1.pericope_label: Up, make us gods: the golden calf, the altar, and the feast to the LORD

schools.summary: Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan that the appointed time had elapsed and Jarchi's explanation that the people miscounted, taking the day of the ascent as one of the forty, has Aaron perceive that they would not be dissuaded and were determined at all events to have a visible image, and reports the Targums that he saw Hur slain before him for reproving the idolatry and feared for his own life. Calvin will allow the people no excuse, calling it detestable impiety and monstrous madness that they should speak contemptuously of the man carried above the state of terrestrial life for their sakes; he grants Aaron's subterfuge but refuses it as an excuse, asking why, if he meant no harm, he did not order the gold thrown into a chest rather than take it into his own hands, makes him the pattern of all who will not maintain what is right but bargain and compromise until they succumb altogether, and marks the people's diligence in appearing at the very dawn, asking what is to be said of our sloth if unbelievers are driven so headlong.

Henry dates the outbreak to the thirty-ninth day of the forty and observes that the people had been given that time to meditate on what was already delivered while some spent it contriving how to break the laws they had received and to forestall those still to come. He adds a second cause, the fury of a multitude corrupted by a few who lie in wait to deceive, so that many were carried down the stream who would never have thought of it themselves, and draws the warning that those with charge of others, as magistrates, ministers and masters of families, should not absent themselves without cause lest Satan get advantage.

Ellicott notes the literary seam, that after seven chapters of ritual directions the writer resumes his narrative and returns from the mount to the plain, and reports the suggestion that these three chapters form a distinct composition inserted between the thirty-first and the thirty-fifth; he calls it a reasonable conjecture that Aaron meant to prevent the idolatry by demanding a sacrifice the people would be unwilling to make, observes that the calculation failed since not the slightest objection was offered, argues that the disputed word means he bound it in a bag on the authority of Gesenius, Rosenmüller and Fürst since a graving tool will not suit a clause calling the image molten, and notes that Aaron, having yielded once, was carried from one compliance to another. Keil and Delitzsch put Aaron's fall plainly, that instead of opposing the proposal and raising the people's despondency into living faith by pointing to the great deeds through which Jehovah had proved himself faithful, he succumbed with them, and describe the feast with its offerings, its eating and drinking, its sports and antiphonal singing.

Clarke reports a long controversy over the term rendered graving tool, some making it a mould, others a garment or cloth or apron, others a purse or bag, others a graver, and supposes himself that a mould was made and the form afterwards finished with chisel and graver; he observes the irony that ornaments granted by God's own providence should be abused to the basest purpose, that the people's bent to idolatry outran even their love of dress, and explains the meal from the ritual, the burnt offerings being wholly consumed while the peace offerings became food once the blood was poured out. Wesley finds them weary of waiting twice over, for the promised land and for the return of Moses, remarks how slightingly they speak of him, reports the view that Aaron's demand was designed to crush the proposal since pride would refuse what covetousness might have allowed while noting that he said not one word to discountenance it, and insists that the people did not mean to terminate their worship in the image but made it a representation of the true God, which excuses them no more than it excuses those who plead the same today.

debates: Whether Aaron meant to prevent the idolatry: Ellicott and the view Wesley reports both take the demand for the earrings as a device to divert the people, while Calvin grants the subterfuge but refuses it as an excuse and Keil and Delitzsch call it plain succumbing

What the disputed word in the fourth verse means: Clarke reports mould, garment, purse and graver as rival renderings and settles on a mould finished with the graver, while Ellicott follows Gesenius and others in reading he bound it in a bag, on the ground that a graving tool cannot precede a molten image
outliers: Ellicott reports the suggestion that these three chapters are a distinct composition inserted between the thirty-first and the thirty-fifth
Gill preserves the Targumic tradition that Aaron saw Hur killed before him for reproving the people, which would put his compliance under duress
Wesley presses the parallel between the calf as a representation of the true God and the same plea made by later image-worshippers

7.pericope_label: Go, get thee down: the disowning of the people and the intercession of Moses

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Septuagint and the Targum add the word quickly to the command and that the idolatry had begun the day before, observes that Moses uses his own interest in a covenant God and that a good man will be concerned for God's honour among his people's enemies, cites the Targum's paraphrase of let me alone as leave off thy prayer and do not cry for them before me, and denies that any thought or determination of God is alterable, holding that what changes is the outward dispensation of his providence. Calvin agrees that so speedy a transgression aggravates the crime and that the plea put forward as a colouring for their ungodliness is alleged last as the climax of the sin; he makes the disowning the sorest of trials for Moses, who had thought all secure when the covenant was engraven on tables and now hears it violated and almost annihilated, holds that the prayer sprang from faith although it seems to fight against the very word of God, and observes that the patriarchs are named not as patrons whose voice might help but because the promise was lodged with them and transmitted as an inheritance.

Henry asks why the news was delayed and answers that God could have told Moses at the first step and sent him down to prevent it, but suffered it to come to this height for wise and holy ends and then sent him to punish it, adding that it is no reproach to God's holiness to suffer sin, since he knows how to restrain it and how to make it serve his own glory. He takes the three charges in order: that they had corrupted themselves, sin being a self-corruption since every man is tempted when drawn aside of his own lust; that they had turned aside out of the way, sin being a deviation from duty into a by-path; and that they had turned aside quickly.

Ellicott notes that the imperative is emphatic and implies urgency and that Moses, hidden by the thick cloud on the summit, knew nothing of what had happened in the plain; he glosses the disowning word exactly, thine and no longer mine since they have broken the covenant, observes that the phrase stiff-necked occurs here for the first time and rather means perverse than obstinate, the metaphor being taken from a horse that stiffens his neck against the rein, and denies that let me alone is a command to abstain from deprecation, calling it an intimation that deprecation might change God's purpose and noting that Moses was tried by an offer which would have exalted him at the people's expense. Keil and Delitzsch make the haste of the apostasy an aggravation which rendered the ingratitude to their Redeemer the more glaring, and give the Hebrew of the beseeching as the stroking of God's face.

Clarke reads the disowning as disinheritance, the people having become abominable in conduct so that God disowns them and they forfeit his protection, turns the passage against the image-worship of his own day, suspects that stiff-necked alludes to the neck of the very ox they had been worshipping, observes that the Omnipotent here represents himself as unable to act in judgment unless his creature desist from praying and compares Abraham pleading for Sodom, and holds that the repenting is spoken merely after the manner of men who, having formed a purpose, are diverted from it by strong reasons. Wesley presses the quickness of the fall, glosses stiff-necked as unapt to come under the yoke of the divine law, asks what Moses could have done to hinder God and answers that God speaks after the manner of men who would have none intercede for those they mean to punish, and so puts an honour upon prayer, reads the appeal as taking the hint God had given, and draws the plain lesson that God suffers himself to be prevailed with by humble believing importunity.

debates: What let me alone means: Clarke takes it as the Omnipotent representing himself unable to act while his creature prays, Ellicott as an intimation that deprecation might change the purpose and a trial offering Moses his own aggrandisement, Wesley as a form of speech after the manner of men which puts an honour upon prayer, and Gill with the Targum as a plain prohibition of prayer

In what sense God repented: Gill denies that any determination of God is alterable and refers the change to the outward dispensation of providence, while Clarke takes the word as spoken merely after the manner of men diverted from a purpose by strong reasons
outliers: Ellicott notes that the phrase stiff-necked, afterwards so common in the Old Testament, occurs here for the first time, and prefers perverse to obstinate as its sense
Clarke suspects that the epithet alludes to the neck of the ox the people had just been worshipping
Calvin insists that the patriarchs are named in the plea not as patrons whose intercession is sought but as the men with whom the promise was lodged

15.pericope_label: The two tables, the noise in the camp, and the breaking and burning of the calf

schools.summary: Gill says the tables were not the work of angels or men, places Joshua low enough on the mount to be ignorant of the people's doings and too high to be among them, notes with Ellicott that what Moses saw was the calf already mentioned and dances not mentioned before, and observes that the calf was melted into a mass and lost its form. Calvin observes that God left the tables untouched in Moses' hands even after pronouncing sentence against the people, draws from the shouting heard so far off how intemperately they raged and how the devil bewitches men so that dissolute licentiousness passes for pious ardour, argues from the praise given to Moses' anger that the Stoic paradox that all passions are vicious must be abandoned while granting that men led by nature are never angry without vice, and alone hesitates over the punishment, which might seem cruel in infecting the bowels of the people with the corruption of their crime and driving them to despair.

Henry calls it a favour that Moses was trusted with the tables, common stone though they were, more valuable than all the precious stones on Aaron's breastplate, and holds that God wrote the commandments without the ministry of man or angel. He describes the arrangement on the mount, Moses in the cloud as in the presence-chamber and Joshua waiting in the antechamber, alone for forty days and fed, it is likely, with manna, yet not weary of waiting as the people were, and coming down only when Moses came.

Ellicott notes that Babylonian and Assyrian tablets are inscribed on both sides, observes that Deuteronomy says more exactly that the tables were in his two hands, reports Rosenmüller's view that only their size and shape were prescribed while holding the natural sense to be that God fashioned them himself, which was not the case with the second tables, fills in Joshua's forty days on the mountain and perhaps in a cleft of the rock, presses the Hebrew of the three clauses so that the sense is the voice neither of those who cry for victory nor of those who cry for defeat but simply of those who cry, says the tables were broken in righteous indignation and perhaps also of design, notes that Oriental dancing of this kind was uniformly lascivious, and has Moses rally a number of the people to his side before laying hold of the calf. Keil and Delitzsch give the process of destruction exactly, the fire calcining the wooden centre and melting the golden coating, what was left being ground to powder and strewed on the water.

Clarke finds the writing on both sides unusual, since in ancient times the two sides of one substance were never written over, and reports the rabbinic supposition that the letters were cut through so as to be legible on either face; he turns the workmanship doctrinal, that God alone is the author of law and alone can write it on the heart, which he takes as the spirit of the new covenant, finds Joshua's guess natural to a military man who hearing a confused noise supposed the camp attacked, offers two accounts of the breaking of the tables, distress of spirit or an emblem that the covenant was as broken as the stones, meets the objection that gold could not be stamped to dust by referring to Deuteronomy, and marks the contempt of making them drink their god. Wesley takes the two sides to mean some commandments on one table and some on the other, folded like a book to be laid in the ark, remarks that this was very probably the first writing in the world, denies that it breaches the law of meekness to show displeasure at wickedness since those are angry and sin not who are angry at sin only, and draws the lesson that the calf was reduced to atoms that it might be as near nothing as could be.

debates: What the writing on both sides means: Clarke reports the rabbinic view that the letters were cut through the stone so as to be legible on either face, Ellicott compares Babylonian and Assyrian tablets, and Wesley takes it of some commandments on one table and some on the other, folded like a book

Whether God fashioned the tables themselves: Ellicott reports Rosenmüller for the view that only their size and shape were prescribed, but prefers the natural sense that God made them, noting that the second tables were otherwise

Why Moses broke the tables: Clarke allows distress of spirit but prefers a deliberate emblem that the covenant was as broken as the stones, Ellicott says righteous indignation and perhaps design, Wesley that he meant to awaken the people by a strong expression of passion
outliers: Calvin uses the praise given to Moses' anger as an argument against the Stoic paradox that all the passions are vicious
Calvin alone hesitates over the making of the people drink the powdered calf, as a punishment that infects them with the corruption of their own crime and might drive them to despair
Wesley notes that the writing on the tables was very probably the first writing in the world

21.pericope_label: Moses calls Aaron to account, and the Levites are consecrated by the sword

schools.summary: Gill grounds the questioning in the trust committed to Aaron with Hur, notes the respectful address of a younger brother who was nevertheless chief ruler, lists what Aaron ought to have said instead of complying, denies that naked can mean stripped of earrings or of armour, places Moses in the gate as the usual place of assembly and judgment, and insists that the orders were not the effect of heat and passion but came expressly from God. Calvin puts Aaron's fault as a principle, that a man possessed of power seems to permit the evil he does not prevent, grants that the modesty of his opening is right enough but calls the excuse frivolous, admits that the command to the Levites may seem cruel and inhuman while denying it excessive if we reflect how much graver it is to profane the worship of God than to injure men, holds the slaughter of three thousand a reminder to the rest that all had deserved the same, and takes the verse about consecration as added to explain why the Levites went through with it.

Henry says Moses begins with Aaron as God began with Adam, because he was the principal person though not first in the transgression but drawn into it, and marks the difference in the treatment, that Aaron was reproved and not cut off like the ringleaders, since much is to be made between those who rush presumptuously into sin and those who through infirmity are surprised into it; he adds that Aaron deserved to be cut off and would have been but for the intercession recorded in Deuteronomy.

Ellicott asks how Aaron acquitted himself of a commission to advise, direct and control the people, notes that most modern commentators prefer licentious or unruly to naked while defending the received rendering, since in the lewd dancing of idolatrous orgies garments were cast aside as the Egyptian monuments show, marks the sequence by which the revel continued after the idol was seized and Aaron shamed so that a third and crowning step had to be taken, holds that Moses felt himself divinely commissioned and that trial was unnecessary where the offence was being openly committed, and explains that a brave behaviour would be accepted as a consecration winning the tribe a semi-priestly character, made good when the Levites were appointed to the sanctuary in place of the firstborn. Keil and Delitzsch will not allow even weakness to acquit Aaron of bringing so great a sin upon the people.

Clarke says in one line that if Aaron had been firm this evil might have been prevented, observes that he pleads the seditious spirit of the people as though obliged to accede, calls the account of the calf coming out of the fire a silly and ridiculous subterfuge and reports that the Targum of Jonathan makes a similar excuse for him, reports the Targum that the people were stripped of the holy crown bearing the divine name while preferring the sense that they were reduced to a helpless and wretched state abandoned by God among their enemies, supposes an entrenched camp with two gates, takes the three thousand for the chief transgressors who by having other gods lost the divine protection, and glosses the consecration as filling the hand to the Lord. Wesley reads the question to Aaron as taking for granted that something more than ordinary prevailed with him, asks whether he could not have opposed God's threatenings to theirs, says it is natural to us to transfer our guilt and that Aaron extenuates his share childishly, catches the imagery of the two standards set up in opposition, and reads the order to the Levites narrowly, as reaching only those found abroad in the street of the camp.

debates: What naked means in the twenty-fifth verse: Gill denies it can mean stripped of earrings or of armour, Clarke reports the Targum of the holy crown but prefers a helpless and abandoned state, and Ellicott notes that most moderns render licentious or unruly while defending the received sense from the practice of idolatrous dancing

How far the order to the Levites reached: Clarke takes the three thousand for the chief transgressors, Wesley restricts the slaying to those found abroad in the street since those retired into their tents might be hoped ashamed, and Ellicott holds all who had committed the idolatry justly forfeit
outliers: Henry distinguishes between overtaking a fault that flees from us and being overtaken in a fault we flee from, and applies it to the difference between Aaron and the ringleaders
Clarke reports that the Targum of Jonathan repeats Aaron's own excuse about the calf coming out of the fire, so that the subterfuge survived into the paraphrase
Calvin insists the slaughter was not satisfaction before God but useful to efface the memory of the guilt and profitable as an example

30.pericope_label: Peradventure I shall make atonement: the plea, the refusal, and the angel promised

schools.summary: Gill dates the sequence from the rabbis, the tables broken on the seventeenth, the calf burnt on the eighteenth and the intercession made on the nineteenth, keeps to what forgiveness would accomplish, that it would redound to God's glory and lay the people under obligation to fear and serve him, and takes the plaguing of some later stroke and not of the three thousand already slain. Calvin sees a double purpose in the address to the survivors, consolation lest they fall into despair and a reminder of the enormity of their sin so that they may come as humble suppliants; he observes that God adapts himself to the comprehension of the human mind in speaking of blotting out, since hypocrites profess his name so plausibly that they are not reckoned aliens until he openly renounces them, takes the appointment of the angel as the sure sign of reconciliation and rejects as a poor exposition the view that it was merely such an angel as was assigned to heathen nations, and reads the last verse as attributing to God what Moses had already related of the slaughter, lest any should think he had smitten them with immoderate severity.

Henry has Moses tell the survivors plainly that they have sinned a great sin, lest those spared should suppose that exemption from the capital punishment meant exemption from guilt, and draws the ministerial rule that the work of ministers is to show people their sins and the greatness of their sins, since a great sin calls for great sorrow because it puts men in great danger.

Ellicott notes that returning to the Lord means re-ascending Sinai to the place of the forty days, that gods of gold should rather be a god of gold since the plural is one of dignity, and explains the broken sentence as aposiopesis, some phrase such as well and good being left unspoken after the word sin, with parallels in Daniel, Luke, John and Romans and the remark that the usage is common among Orientals; he holds that Moses rose to the height of self-abnegation St Paul afterwards reached, sets the divine answer beside the word of Ezekiel that the soul which sins shall die and argues that a mere man cannot take other men's sins upon him, observes that the promise of the angel is as nearly as possible a repetition of the original one, and denies that a pestilence is meant at the close, taking it of sufferings of various kinds. Keil and Delitzsch set the exchange out as it stands.

Clarke gives the book a concrete sense, supposing that part of the forty days was spent regulating the muster-roll of the tribes so that to be blotted out is to be struck from that register, expands the divine answer into a speech that all God's conduct is regulated by justice and in no case shall the innocent suffer for the guilty, observes that the word place is not in the text and is rightly omitted since Moses never led the people into the land but only towards it, and reports the Jewish saying that no affliction ever befell Israel without some particle of the dust of the golden calf in it. Wesley catches the wording of the confession, that Moses does not call them God's people but this treacherous and ungrateful people, supplies the unspoken half of the plea, that if the decree has gone forth Moses is content to perish with them, compares Paul wishing himself accursed for his brethren, takes the angel for a created one employed in the common services of the kingdom so that nothing thereafter was to be expected out of the common road of providence, and concludes that Moses obtained a mitigation of the punishment but could not wholly turn away the wrath.

debates: What the angel promised is: Calvin takes the appointment as the sure sign of reconciliation and rejects the view that it was merely such an angel as heathen nations had, while Wesley reads it as a created angel of the common services of the kingdom, intimating that nothing thereafter would be done out of the common road of providence

What the plaguing at the close refers to: Gill and Wesley take it of a later stroke, pestilence or other calamity, Ellicott of sufferings of various kinds rather than a pestilence, and Calvin of the slaughter of the three thousand already related
outliers: Ellicott identifies the unfinished sentence as aposiopesis and gathers parallels from Daniel, Luke, John and Romans, calling the usage common among Orientals
Clarke supposes the book to be a muster-roll of the tribes drawn up during the forty days, which would give being blotted out a concrete sense
Clarke preserves the Jewish saying that no affliction has ever happened to Israel without some particle of the dust of the golden calf in it
